name: sshkey_curve_nid_to_bits
prose: Maps an OpenSSL elliptic-curve NID to a key size in bits (sshkey.c:604-619; compiled only with WITH_OPENSSL), returning a u_int. NID_X9_62_prime256v1 (415) gives 256, NID_secp384r1 (715) gives 384, and NID_secp521r1 (716) gives 521 only when OPENSSL_HAS_NISTP521 is defined at compile time; any other value, and 716 in a build without that macro, gives 0. It reads no state, allocates nothing and has no side effects.
note: sshkey.c:604-619 read in full. Reviewer 4 (round 15) right that the old text had the wrong NID: NID_secp384r1 is 715 (openssl include/openssl/obj_mac.h:372), not 714; the rounds 1 and 2 reviewers right about the OPENSSL_HAS_NISTP521 condition (612-615).

name: sshkey_ecdsa_bits_to_nid
prose: Maps an ECDSA key size in bits to an OpenSSL curve NID (sshkey.c:621-636; compiled only with WITH_OPENSSL), returning an int. 256 gives NID_X9_62_prime256v1 (415), 384 gives NID_secp384r1 (715), and 521 gives NID_secp521r1 (716) only when OPENSSL_HAS_NISTP521 is defined at compile time; any other value, and 521 in a build without that macro, gives -1. It reads no state, allocates nothing and has no side effects.
note: sshkey.c:621-636 read in full. Corrected NID_secp384r1 from 714 to 715 (obj_mac.h:372, a reviewer claim confirmed); the 521 case depends on OPENSSL_HAS_NISTP521 (629-632).

name: sshkey_ec_nid_to_hash_alg
prose: Chooses the digest used with an ECDSA curve (sshkey.c:655-670; compiled only with WITH_OPENSSL), returning an int. It computes the key size with sshkey_curve_nid_to_bits(nid); if that size is not positive (an unsupported NID, including NID_secp521r1 in a build without OPENSSL_HAS_NISTP521) it returns -1. Otherwise a size up to 256 gives SSH_DIGEST_SHA256, a size up to 384 gives SSH_DIGEST_SHA384, and any larger size gives SSH_DIGEST_SHA512; so NID 415 gives SHA256, NID 715 gives SHA384 and NID 716 (when supported) gives SHA512. The symbolic constants are SSH_DIGEST_SHA256, SHA384 and SHA512 (digest.h:27-29 defines them as 2, 3 and 4 in this tree). It allocates nothing and has no side effects.
note: sshkey.c:655-670 read in full; digest.h:26-29 for the digest constants. Reviewer 4 (round 15) right: NID 714 is not the 384-bit curve (it returns -1), the P-384 NID is 715; the old numeric values for the digest ids (3, 4, 5) were wrong, the file defines SHA256=2, SHA384=3, SHA512=4.

name: unpack_revinfo
prose: Parses a revocation-info string of the form time[,reason[,argument]] used by the ca application (apps/ca.c:2567-2676; the real name is unpack_revinfo, with output pointers prevtm, preason, phold, pinvtm and the input str; the slice shows its second half). It returns 1 on success and 0 on any failure, printing a message to bio_err. It duplicates str (failure: message and 0), splits it at the first two commas, and, when prevtm is non-NULL, allocates an ASN1 UTC time into *prevtm and sets it from the time text (an allocation or invalid-date failure returns 0, leaving the already allocated *prevtm in place for the caller, since the function does not free it). When a reason text is present it is matched case-insensitively against the table of reason names; an unmatched text gives "invalid reason code" and 0. Reason index 7 becomes OCSP_REVOKED_STATUS_REMOVEFROMCRL; index 8 (hold) needs the argument, parses it as an object identifier with OBJ_txt2obj (missing or invalid: 0) and stores it in *phold when phold is non-NULL, otherwise frees it; indices 9 and 10 need the argument as a GeneralizedTime (missing, allocation failure or invalid: 0) and become key-compromise or CA-compromise respectively. On success it stores the reason code in *preason when preason is non-NULL (it stays -1, meaning no reason, when no reason text was given), transfers the compromise time to *pinvtm when pinvtm is non-NULL, and returns 1; otherwise the compromise time is freed. The duplicate string is always freed. *preason and *pinvtm are written only on success.
note: ca.c:2567-2676 read in full, comments skipped. Packet name make_revoked is not the function in this slice: make_revoked (2474-2523) is a separate function that calls unpack_revinfo (2485) and returns 0, 1 or 2 (2511-2513); the old prose described make_revoked (and so was right about rev==NULL being allowed only if the code at 2474-2523 says so, which I did not recheck). Reviewer 15 saw this same name mismatch; note it as right.

name: ca_main
prose: Middle part of the main function of the openssl ca command (apps/ca.c:311-1362, the real name is ca_main; this slice 554-807 starts after option parsing and ends in the database-update step). The function keeps ret initialised to 1 (346), sets it to 0 for -help (366) and again at 1338 before the common end label, so a path that jumps to end without setting ret returns 1. In this part it takes the remaining arguments, loads the configuration file (failure: goto end), loads modules for a non-default config, finds the CA section (the section option or the default_ca setting) and optionally the oid_file and the OID section, loads random state, reads the string mask, UTF8 setting and unique_subject setting. If a serial-status query (ser_status) was requested it loads the database, builds its index and prints an error if the status check does not return 1, then goes to end; nothing on this path (606-623) sets ret to 0, so it ends with the initial value 1 even when the lookup succeeds, which a reviewer pointed out. Otherwise it reads the passphrase option, loads the CA private key and zeros the passphrase, and unless selfsign applies without spkac, self-signed certificate file or CRL generation it loads the CA certificate and checks that it matches the key (mismatch: goto end). It then reads the preserve, msie_hack, name option, cert option and extension copy settings (a bad value goes to end), checks that the new-certs directory exists when requests are present, loads the database and validates every entry (revoked entries need a valid revocation date through make_revoked, expiry dates must have the right format, serials need an even number of hex digits), builds its index, and, when updating the database was requested, calls do_updatedb and on a change saves and rotates the index files (errors go to end). The rest of the function (extension loading, certification of requests, CRL generation) is outside this slice.
note: ca.c:554-806 read with BIO_printf lines skipped, plus ca.c:346, 366 and 1338-1362 grep context. Reviewer 17 right: the ser_status path (606-623) reaches end with ret still 1; the old prose claim that success returns 0 was wrong for that path. The packet name main does not exist, the function is ca_main (311). Lines 807-1338 were not read.

name: ciphers_main
prose: Second half of the openssl ciphers command (apps/ciphers.c:91-287; the real function is ciphers_main, which takes argc and argv; this slice lies in its listing loop, 254-287). The function starts with ret equal to 1, sets it to 0 for -help (121), when a -convert name is printed (188) and at the end of a successful listing (277), and returns ret at 286. After option parsing it uses a single optional positional argument as the cipher list, creates an SSL_CTX, sets the minimum and maximum protocol versions, installs the dummy PSK callback or the dummy SRP setup when those options were given, sets the TLS 1.3 ciphersuites and the cipher list when given (any failure goes to err, which prints the OpenSSL error queue to bio_err and then reaches end with ret 1), creates an SSL object, and takes the cipher stack with SSL_get1_supported_ciphers when use_supported is set and SSL_get_ciphers otherwise. Without verbose it prints the cipher names separated by colons and a newline; with verbose it loops over the ciphers, skipping NULL entries, prints for Verbose (capital V) the numeric id (a short form for ids whose top byte is 0x03), prints the standard name with -stdname (UNKNOWN when none) and then the description. At end it frees the cipher stack only when use_supported is set, frees the SSL_CTX and the SSL object and returns ret; the -convert path and early option errors also reach end with ctx, ssl and sk still NULL, which the free calls tolerate.
note: ciphers.c:150-287 read in full, 91-150 only grepped for ret assignments (97, 121, 188, 277). The packet record was marked dropped and named ciphers; it is a real function, ciphers_main (91), so it is fixed rather than dropped. The old prose "frees the SSL object, the SSL_CTX and, when use_supported was selected, the cipher stack on every return path" is wrong for a return from inside the option loop, if any (not read at 91-150), and the -convert path.

name: cmp_server
prose: Runs the OpenSSL cmp application's built-in mock server loop (apps/cmp.c:3286-3361; built only when sockets and HTTP are available). With the context srv_cmp_ctx it first calls http_server_init for the port and verbosity; if that returns NULL it returns 0. Otherwise, while opt_max_msgs is not positive or fewer than opt_max_msgs messages were handled, each iteration receives one HTTP request with http_server_get_asn1_req. A result of 0 (no request yet) sleeps one second and retries once; on a second such result it clears ret and goes to the label next without counting a message. A result of -1 (fatal) breaks out of the loop with ret then equal to 0 because of the post-increment at 3315. For a received message it counts it, sets ret to 0, and if a request was parsed checks the path: a path other than "" or "pkix/" sends a 404 status, logs and goes to next with ret 0. Otherwise it calls OSSL_CMP_CTX_server_perform with the global client context cmp_ctx (not srv_cmp_ctx): a NULL response sends a 500 status and breaks with ret 0; otherwise it sends the response with http_server_send_asn1_resp and sets ret to its result, and a zero result breaks out of the loop. At next, when ret is 0 (a path error, an empty request, or a retry exhausted) it clears the transaction ID and sender nonce of srv_cmp_ctx; this clearing is skipped on the two break paths (send failure and NULL response), a point a reviewer made. When ret is 0, keep-alive is off or the server transaction is not in progress it frees the connection BIO and sets it to NULL. After the loop it frees both BIOs and returns ret: 0 after any break and for an iteration that ended through next with ret 0, and the nonzero result of http_server_send_asn1_resp when the loop ended by the message limit right after a successful send.
note: cmp.c:3286-3361 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 15 right that the send-failure break skips clearing the transaction ID and sender nonce (3342-3343 break before next at 3345); the earlier reviewer was right that the return value is 0 on the NULL-request path when the limit is reached at the end of that iteration (ret stays 0 at 3318). The old claim that the response comes from srv_cmp_ctx was wrong: the call uses cmp_ctx (3330).

name: cmp_main
prose: Later part of the main function of the openssl cmp command (apps/cmp.c:3673-4013, the real name is cmp_main; this slice 3744-4008 starts after option parsing). ret starts at 0 (3679, "failure"), becomes the result of the config/option handling (the code at 3717-3737 sets it to -1 for a bad option or -help usage in lines not read in full) and is set to 0 at 3737 before this slice. It sets up the UI method (batch), loads the optional engine (failure: goto err), the log callback and verbosity, and checks the TLS and port option combinations (several incompatible combinations go to err). When no -reqout_only is given and the mock server or -port is used, it builds the server context; with -port it runs ret = cmp_server(srv_cmp_ctx) and goes to err. With -reqout_only it rejects -port, ignores some other options and sets reqout. It then sets up the client context (failure: err) and runs the command opt_repeat times: IR, KUR, CR and P10CR set ret to 1 only when a certificate is returned, RR takes the result of OSSL_CMP_exec_RR_ses, genm takes do_genm and an unknown command leaves ret unchanged. If the CMP status is below accepted it sets ret to 0, or to 1 when the request was only written for -reqout_only, and goes to err. After print_status it saves or deletes the validated server certificate (failure sets ret to 0), goes to err if ret is 0, resets ret to 0, saves the extra certs, and for the enrolment commands the new chain, certificate, CA certificates and, with centralkeygen, the new private key (each failure goes to err with ret 0), then reinitialises the context (failure: err). After the loop ret is 1 (so zero repetitions also give 1). At err it cleanses the password and secret option strings, prints the CMP error queue when ret is not 1, frees the context, mock server, certConf store, TLS info, verify params, engine and config, closes the log and returns EXIT_FAILURE only when ret is 0 and EXIT_SUCCESS for every other value, including -1 (the -help or bad-option marker) and the nonzero value returned by cmp_server.
note: cmp.c:3741-4013 read in full with message lines skipped; 3673-3740 only grepped for ret. Reviewer 17 right: the final line returns ret == 0 ? EXIT_FAILURE : EXIT_SUCCESS (4012) so ret -1 gives EXIT_SUCCESS; packet name main does not exist, the function is cmp_main (3673); the old statement that all error paths include cleansing is right for the goto err paths but the early part of the function (not read) may return before err.

name: cms_main
prose: Late part of the main function of the openssl cms command (apps/cms.c:342-1395, the real name is cms_main; this slice 1077-1377 holds the encrypt/sign/verify work and the end label). Return code ret starts at 1, is set to 0 for -help (398), to 2 at 871 (the argument-loading stage), to 3 at 1045 before the CMS structure is created, to 4 at 1232 after it, and the function returns ret at 1395. In this slice the CMS structure is built by operation: data, digest, compress, encrypt (partial structure, then one recipient per certificate with optional key parameters and wrap cipher, then a secret-key recipient and a password recipient, then CMS_final unless streaming), encrypted-data encrypt, sign-receipt, or sign/resign (signers loaded one by one: a failure to load a signer certificate or key sets ret to 2, other failures keep ret 3). Any failure inside these steps goes to end with ret 3, including a NULL cms at 1227-1229. After creation ret is 4: decrypt (with secret key, private key, password), data out, uncompress, digest verify, encrypted-data decrypt, verify (a failure sets ret to verify_err + 32 when -verify_retcode is given, else stays 4; failure to save signers sets 5), verify receipt, or output. In output, with -noout it only prints when requested; otherwise it writes SMIME, PEM or DER with the matching function whose result is put into ret, and a result of 0 or less sets ret to 6 and goes to end (an unknown output format also goes to end with the current ret). A path that reaches the line ret = 0 at 1353 returns 0. At end it prints the OpenSSL error queue when ret is non-zero and frees the certificate stacks, parameters, keys, strings and objects it owns. The signer certificate and key are freed only at the end of each loop iteration or in the final cleanup, so on an error inside the loop they are released by the end code.
note: cms.c:1040-1360 read in full with message lines skipped, 342-398 grepped, 1360-1395 not read (the rest of the cleanup). Reviewer 17 wrong that a NULL cms path does not set ret to 3: ret = 3 is set at 1045, so goto end at 1229 returns 3. Reviewer 15's claim that signer and key are not freed on several error paths is not supported by what I read (the end label cleanup was only partly read, so I make no claim for those two objects). The old claim that secret_key and secret_keyid are not freed when absorbed matches 1105-1106.

name: cms_main
prose: Option-processing part of the main function of the openssl cms command (apps/cms.c:342-1395, the real name is cms_main; this slice 562-822 lies in the option switch and the checks that follow it). ret is 1 from the start, so every goto end or opthelp reached here (a missing or duplicated argument, a failed allocation or push, an invalid object identifier, an engine, key-format, certificate or config load failure, a bad digest, cipher or wrap-cipher name, or an inconsistent option combination) returns 1 after the queued OpenSSL errors are printed. The cases in this slice store the options: CA path flags, input and content files, receipt-request lists, name options, secret key and key id (hex decoded; a repeated option or a bad hex string is an error), password, content type (OBJ_txt2obj), engine, passphrase source, headers (to, from, subject), certs output, digest, signer and its key (each -signer pushes the previous pair onto the signers and keys lists; -inkey without a signer is an error), originator, key format, recipient certificate (loaded and pushed when the operation is encrypt, otherwise remembered as the recipient file), the cipher name from an unknown option, key parameters (-keyopt, with the key index computed from the signers/keys or recipient count), verify parameters, random options, provider and config options and the wrap cipher. After the loop it loads the random state, looks up the digest and ciphers, and checks the combinations: receipt recipients without signers, receipts or multiple signers or keys without -sign, and CAdES with no-attributes or with verification-disabling flags (all errors, ret 1). With signing operations it then validates -inkey/-signer pairing. The body of the checks past line 822 and the operation itself were not read here.
note: cms.c:555-830 read with message lines skipped; 830-870 not read. Reviewer 15 and 17 comments are for the other slice of the same function. The packet name cms_main is right. The old prose described the whole function (operations and return codes 2 to 6) which this slice does not contain; claims about return 2 at 871 are outside this slice.

name: set_hex
prose: Static helper of the openssl enc command (apps/enc.c:849-877; the real name is set_hex, not hex2bin) that decodes a hexadecimal string into a fixed-size byte buffer. It takes the string length n and the capacity size*2 hex digits. If n is larger it prints "hex string is too long, ignoring excess" to bio_err and only uses the first size*2 characters; if smaller it prints "hex string is too short, padding with zero bytes to length". It then sets all size bytes of out to zero and decodes the characters one by one: a character that is not a hex digit prints "non-hex digit" and returns 0 at once; the high nibble of each byte is stored first (out[i/2] = digit << 4, which overwrites) and the low nibble is OR-ed in. An odd number of digits leaves the last nibble in the high half of its byte. At a failure the buffer holds the zeroed bytes plus the digits already written, including a high nibble stored for the failing digit's byte only if its first digit was valid and the failing digit is the second one. It returns 1 on success (including both warning cases) and 0 on a non-hex digit. It allocates nothing and does not modify in.
note: enc.c:849-877 read in full. Packet name hex2bin does not exist, the function is set_hex (849). Reviewer 15 right: on a non-hex digit at an odd index the high nibble of that byte was already stored by the previous iteration, so out keeps a partial byte.

name: self_test_events
prose: Callback of the openssl fipsinstall command for provider self-test events (apps/fipsinstall.c:973-1021; the slice 808-1021 also holds the tail of fipsinstall_main). It returns an int and ignores its arg. It locates the phase, description and type parameters in params; if any of the three is missing or is not a UTF8 string it returns 0. When logging is enabled (self_test_log) it prints a line at the start phase and at the pass or fail phases (the exact text is in message lines not read). If the phase is the corrupt phase and a corruption description or type was configured, then a configured description that differs from desc, or a configured type that differs from type, makes it return 1; when every configured selector matches it returns 0 (which makes the self-test corrupt its result). In every other case, including the corrupt phase with no selector configured, other phases, and a corrupt phase whose selectors do not match, it returns 1. It allocates and frees nothing.
note: fipsinstall.c:973-1021 read in full, comments skipped; 808-971 (tail of fipsinstall_main) read separately and not described here. Reviewer 1 right that missing or mistyped parameters are handled by returning 0 (980-991); reviewer 15 right that with no selectors configured the code returns 1 (1005-1007 condition false, falls to end at 1017-1018).

name: process_cert_request
prose: Mock CMP server callback that answers a certificate request (apps/lib/cmp_mock_srv.c:298-430). It takes the custom context from srv_ctx and returns NULL, raising CMP_R_NULL_ARGUMENT, if that context, cert_req, certOut, chainOut or caPubs is NULL; the outputs are not touched in that case. If ctx->sendError is 1 or equals the body type of the request it raises an error and returns NULL, again without touching the three outputs. Otherwise it sets *certOut, *chainOut and *caPubs to NULL. If a poll count is configured and the current poll count is 0 it duplicates the request into ctx->req (NULL result on allocation failure) and returns a new status info with the waiting status; otherwise it resets the current poll count to 0 once it has reached the configured count. For a CR request that carries a certProfile entry in the general-info it requires exactly one first string equal to "profile1" (a failure or mismatch returns NULL with the outputs NULL). For a KUR with a reference certificate and a CRMF message it requires the old-certificate id and checks it against the reference (missing: NULL with CMP_R_MISSING_CERTID; mismatch: NULL with CMP_R_WRONG_CERTID). Then it duplicates ctx->certOut into *certOut when set, checks whether central key generation was requested (a negative answer goes to err), and for central key generation duplicates ctx->keyOut and installs it as the new private key in the server's CMP context, failing to err if no key is configured or either step fails. It then up-refs ctx->chainOut and ctx->caPubsOut into *chainOut and *caPubs when those are set and duplicates ctx->statusOut into the returned status info when set. A failure up to that point goes to err, which frees and NULLs all three outputs and returns NULL. If statusOut is NULL it returns NULL (si stays NULL) without going through err, so the outputs may be set (owned by the caller) with a NULL return; otherwise the returned status info and the outputs are owned by the caller.
note: cmp_mock_srv.c:298-430 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (early NULL returns before 323 leave outputs untouched; a NULL statusOut returns NULL at 420 with outputs set); reviewer 15 right that the central-keygen path (395-405) exists, may fail and then frees all outputs. The old prose's claim that the allocation failure after the outputs are set frees all three is right only for the paths that go to err.

name: log_set_verbosity
prose: Sets the global log verbosity of the openssl apps (apps/lib/log.c:16-25) and returns an int. If level is below LOG_EMERG or above LOG_TRACE it calls trace_log_message with category -1, program name prog, level LOG_ERR and the text "Invalid verbosity level %d", leaves the stored verbosity unchanged and returns 0. Otherwise it stores level in the static variable verbosity and returns 1. The error text is only printed when the current verbosity is at least LOG_ERR: trace_log_message (71-108) returns early without output when verbosity is less than the message level, and with category -1 it does not use the trace channel.
note: log.c:14-108 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 15 right that the invalid-level message is not always emitted (log.c:95-98 returns when verbosity < level); reviewers 1 and 2 right that the unchanged verbosity and the traced message belong in the description.

name: shacrypt
prose: Computes the SHA-256 or SHA-512 crypt hash of a password for openssl passwd (apps/passwd.c:501-780; the real name is shacrypt, with arguments passwd, magic and salt, all NUL-terminated strings; the slice shows its middle and end). It returns a pointer to its own static buffer out_buf (not a caller-supplied one) or NULL. It returns NULL, before touching out_buf, when magic is not exactly one character or is neither '5' (SHA-256, 32-byte digest) nor '6' (SHA-512, 64-byte digest), and when salt starts with "rounds=" but the number is not followed by '$'. A valid rounds prefix is parsed with strtoul, clamped to 1000..999999999 and marks the rounds as custom; the salt then starts after the '$'. The salt is copied truncated to 16 characters. The result string is built as "$<magic>$", then "rounds=<n>$" for a custom round count, then the salt; if that string is longer than 3 + 17 (when custom) + the salt length it goes to err and returns NULL. It then runs the standard SHA-crypt steps with two digest contexts: hash of password, salt and password; the password length of that block; the bits of the password length; the P sequence (digest of the password repeated password-length times, stretched to the password length), the S sequence (digest of 16 + first digest byte copies of the salt, stretched to the salt length) and the given number of rounds that mix the previous digest, P and S. Any failed digest call or allocation (EVP_MD_CTX_new, EVP_DigestInit_ex, EVP_DigestUpdate, EVP_DigestFinal_ex, OPENSSL_zalloc of the P and S arrays) goes to err, which frees the contexts and the arrays and returns NULL. On success it frees the contexts and arrays, appends '$' and the digest in the crypt base-64 form (43 characters for SHA-256 and 86 for SHA-512 in the fixed permutations) and returns out_buf. Since out_buf is static, a later call overwrites an earlier result. OPENSSL_zalloc is called with passwd_len and salt_len, so a zero-length password or salt asks for zero bytes; whether that allocation succeeds depends on CRYPTO_zalloc, which I did not read.
note: passwd.c:501-780 read in full, comments skipped. The old prose, which treated out_buf as caller-supplied, is wrong (515: static char out_buf[3 + 17 + 17 + 86 + 1]); the old claim that the early returns leave out_buf untouched is right (536-567 happen before 591). The packet name sha_crypt does not exist, the function is shacrypt.

name: do_passwd
prose: Hashes one password for openssl passwd and prints it (apps/passwd.c:782-852; it returns int, 1 on success, 0 when the random salt cannot be made). If passed_salt is 0 it chooses the salt length from mode (8 for md5, apr1 and aixmd5, 16 for sha256 and sha512; any other mode trips an assertion), allocates a buffer of that length plus one only when *salt_malloc_p is NULL (setting both *salt_p and *salt_malloc_p to it) and otherwise writes into the existing *salt_p without checking its size, so a caller-supplied buffer must hold at least saltlen+1 bytes (reviewer 15 right). It fills the salt with RAND_bytes (a failure returns 0 through end, leaving any allocated buffer for the caller) and maps each byte to the crypt alphabet with the 6 low bits, then NUL-terminates. If the password is longer than pw_maxlen it prints a warning to bio_err unless quiet is set and truncates passwd in place. It then hashes with md5crypt using magic "1" for md5, "apr1" for apr1 or "" for aixmd5, or with shacrypt using "5" or "6", on the salt at *salt_p; the hash is only checked with an assertion, so in a build without assertions a failed hash would be passed to BIO_printf as NULL. It prints "passwd<TAB>hash" when table is set and reverse is not, "hash<TAB>passwd" when both are set, and "hash" otherwise, each followed by a newline, and returns 1. The caller owns the salt buffer recorded in *salt_malloc_p.
note: passwd.c:782-852 read in full, comments skipped; md5crypt and shacrypt were not re-read for this record (shacrypt was read for another record). The packet precondition omitting the buffer room is a reviewer claim confirmed (804-806, 811).

name: pkcs8_main
prose: Final part of the main function of the openssl pkcs8 command (apps/pkcs8.c:90-406, the real name is pkcs8_main; this slice 302-406 starts inside the encrypt branch of the -topk8 conversion). ret starts at 1 (105); it is set to 0 only for -help (123), after the topk8 branch finished its output (319) and after the normal output at 392; every goto end taken before one of those assignments, including the option-error label opthelp, returns 1. In the -topk8 branch the encryption algorithm (pbe) is built with scrypt, PBES2 or the PBE nid, a NULL one prints an error and goes to end, the password is the -passout value or is read from the terminal (failure goes to end), PKCS8_set0_pbe wraps the key (NULL: the algorithm is freed, error printed, end), and the result is written as PEM or DER; an unknown output format prints "Bad format" and goes to end (ret 1). A topk8 branch with -nocrypt writes the unencrypted PKCS#8 structure in the same way. In the other branch the input is read as PKCS#8 (-nocrypt: a PrivateKeyInfo, PEM or DER; otherwise an encrypted X509_SIG whose password comes from -passin or the terminal and which is decrypted with PKCS8_decrypt); an unsupported input format, a NULL result, a failure to read the password, a decryption failure or a failure of EVP_PKCS82PKEY goes to end with ret 1. It then opens the output file with bio_open_owner (NULL goes to end), writes the key as PEM (traditional form when requested, otherwise PKCS#8) or DER, with an unknown format going to end, and sets ret to 0. The return values of the PEM and DER write calls are not checked in any branch, so a write error still gives ret 0 (reviewer 17 right). At end it frees the X509_SIG, PKCS8 key info, key, cipher, engine, output and input BIOs and the passin and passout strings and returns ret.
note: pkcs8.c:255-406 read in full with message lines skipped; 90-130 read for the option label (opthelp prints "Use -help" and goes to end, 118-121); the early body 130-255 not read. The packet name main does not exist, the function is pkcs8_main (90).

name: req_main
prose: Middle part of the main function of the openssl req command (apps/req.c:283-1108, the real name is req_main; this slice 546-826 runs from the end of option parsing to the loading of the CA files). ret starts at 1 (310), is set to 0 for -help (330) and at 991 and 1077, and the function returns it at 1108; the option-error label opthelp (325-327) prints "Use -help" and goes to end with ret still 1 (so a bad option returns 1, not 0). In this slice: extra arguments go to opthelp; random loading, passphrase options, the config template and the -addext config are loaded (any failure goes to end); the OID file and OID section are added; a given digest is checked (failure goes to opthelp), else default_md is read; the extension sections are test-added (failure goes to end); passin and passout default to the config values; the string mask and UTF8 flag are read. If -key was given the private key is loaded (failure: end); a -newkey together with -key only prints a warning. When a new request is wanted and no key is loaded it reads the key length (default if absent), creates a key generation context (NULL: end), rejects RSA, RSA-PSS or DSA keys under the minimum length (end), warns for oversized RSA or DSA keys, applies the -pkeyopt options (a failure goes to end), generates the key (NULL: end), looks up the key output file in the config when none was given and, when a key was generated or -keyout was given, writes the private key as PEM, retrying up to 3 times on a password problem (failure: end). A -subj subject is parsed (failure: end). When no new request is made it loads an existing request from -in or stdin (NULL: end); in that case pkey can remain NULL when no -key or -newkey was given (reviewer 17 right). Then the -CA/-CAkey files are loaded (failure or key mismatch: end). The rest of the function is outside this slice.
note: req.c:546-830 read in full with message lines skipped, 283-331 for the label and ret (310, 325-331). Reviewer 15 wrong that the bad-option path returns 0: opthelp goes to end with ret 1; reviewer 17 right that pkey may be NULL after loading an existing request (779-786, no key requested).

name: req_main
prose: Final part of the main function of the openssl req command (apps/req.c:283-1108, the real name is req_main; this slice 827-1110 holds the request and certificate creation tail and the end label). ret is 1 until it is set to 0 at 991 (the -noout with nothing else requested path, which jumps to end) or at 1077 (after all output has been written). It creates the request if needed (failure goes to end), sets the subject name (failure: end), prints the subject when verbose, verifies the request when -verify is given (a negative result goes to end, 0 prints an error and goes to end), and for -noout without text, modulus, subject or pubkey returns 0 at once. It opens the output file (NULL: end), writes the public key for -pubkey, and for -text prints the certificate or request with the result stored in ret: a result of 0 means the print failed and the function goes to end with ret equal to 0, so it returns 0 (success status) after a print failure and, since ret is 0, without printing the OpenSSL error queue; a non-zero result leaves ret non-zero until it is reset at 1077, and later failures go to end with that non-zero ret (a nonzero value, normally 1). It then prints the subject, prints the RSA modulus (a missing public key or failed parameter fetch goes to end, ret then holding the earlier text result or 1), writes the request in DER or PEM (a failure goes to end) and the certificate (same), and sets ret to 0. At end it prints the OpenSSL errors when ret is non-zero, frees the configs, BIOs, keys, key context, option stacks, hash table, engines, request, subject, certificates, key and serial, frees passin and passout only when they were not config-owned, and returns ret. The older claim that every error returns 1 is wrong because of the print path; the claim that all objects are freed is right for the end label as shown.
note: req.c:960-1108 read in full with message lines skipped; the stretch 830-960 (request and certificate construction) was not read. Reviewers 15 and 17 right: X509_print_ex or X509_REQ_print_ex returning 0 sets ret to 0 at 1013-1015 and the function goes to end at 1022, returning 0; when -text succeeded ret is the print result (non-zero) at that point and a later failure at 1039, 1046, 1064 or 1074 returns that non-zero value.

name: rsa_main
prose: Second half of the main function of the openssl rsa command (apps/rsa.c:137-428, the real name is rsa_main; this slice 252-428 runs from loading the key to the end label). ret starts at 1 (148) and is set to 0 only for -help (168), for -noout after the checks (327), after a successful legacy-encoding fallback (384) and after a successful OSSL_ENCODER_to_bio (418); the function returns it at 427. Every goto end before those points (including the option-error label opthelp reached from the option loop) returns 1. In this slice it rejects -check with -pubin (end), loads the public key (with a legacy PEM or ASN1 RSA format when pubin is 2) or the private key (NULL: errors printed, end), requires the key to be RSA or RSA-PSS (end otherwise), opens the output with bio_open_owner (NULL: end), and for -text prints the public or private key (a failure goes to end). For -modulus it fetches the "n" parameter and prints it with BN_print, and the return values of EVP_PKEY_get_bn_param and BN_print are not checked, so a failure there does not stop the command (reviewer 15 right). With -check it creates a key context (NULL: end), runs EVP_PKEY_check: a result of 1 prints "RSA key ok", 0 prints "RSA key not ok" and continues, and a negative result prints errors and goes to end. With -noout it ends with ret 0. Otherwise it picks the output type (DER, PEM, MSBLOB or PVK; PVK with a public key input and an unsupported format go to end) and structure, creates an encoder context for the key; when no encoder is available it uses the legacy function try_legacy_encoding for public output (success gives ret 0 and the end; failure and the private-key case return 1). It sets the cipher and passphrase when encrypting, the PVK encryption level (failure: end) and calls OSSL_ENCODER_to_bio, which on failure prints the OpenSSL errors and goes to end with ret 1. At end it frees the encoder context, engine, output, key, cipher and both password strings.
note: rsa.c:137-428 grepped for control flow and read from 247 to 427 with message lines skipped; the start (option loop 137-247) was not read. Reviewer 15 right: the modulus printing is unchecked (292-300). The old claim that EVP_PKEY_check returning 0 only prints is right (315-322).

name: s_server_main
prose: Last part of the main function of the openssl s_server command (apps/s_server.c:1110-2484; the real name is s_server_main, taking argc and argv; this slice 2226-2486 holds the context set-up tail and the end label). ret starts at 1 (1135) and is set to 0 for -help (1242) and at 2445 after the server loop; the function returns ret at 2484, so every goto end before 2445 returns 1. In this slice it finishes the DH parameters (auto DH when none was loaded; a failure of EVP_PKEY_up_ref or SSL_CTX_set0_tmp_dh_pkey goes to end), installs certificates and keys with set_cert_key_stuff for the main context, the optional second context and the second certificate (failure: end), loads a serverinfo file (failure: end), sets the not-resumable callback, the PSK server callback, a PSK identity hint (a failure goes to end) and a PSK session file (open or read failure: end), sets verify callbacks, the session id context (failure: end), cookie callbacks and the servername callbacks when a second context exists, the SRP verifier file (failure: end), client CA lists, the OCSP status callbacks, the keylog file (a non-zero result goes to end), the early-data limits, and, with cert compression, SSL_CTX_compress_certs for ctx and ctx2 where a failure only prints a message and does not stop (reviewer 17 right); it applies the RPK certificate types (failure: end). It then selects rev_body, www_body or sv_body, unlinks a unix socket path when asked, calls do_server and print_stats, and sets ret to 0 unconditionally: the return value of do_server is not used (reviewer 15 right), so the function returns 0 whenever it reached this line. At end it frees the contexts, session, keys, certificates, CRLs, chains, strings, option stacks, verify parameters, engine, and the s_out and s_msg BIOs (setting both globals to NULL) and returns ret.
note: s_server.c:2226-2484 read with message lines skipped; 1110-2225 not read (only the ret assignments at 1135, 1242 and 2445 were checked). Reviewer 15 right (2442-2445 ignore the result of do_server); reviewer 17 right (2411-2416 print and continue without goto end).

name: www_body
prose: Serves one accepted connection for the s_server -www, -WWW and -HTTP modes (apps/s_server.c:3255-3733, int www_body(int s, int stype, int prot, unsigned char *context); the slice 3029-3287 shows only the start of it, after is_retryable and init_ssl_connection). Its result variable ret is initialised to 1 at 3258 and the only other assignment in the function is ret = 1 at 3417 (end of input), so every path I found that reaches its single return at 3732 returns 1, including the error paths: failures to allocate the buffer, the SSL object, the BIOs or the early-data connection go to err with ret still 1, and a clean end of input goes to end. The paths differ only in cleanup: end calls do_ssl_shutdown(con) first, while err does not; both free the read buffer, the SSL BIO, the I/O BIO chain and the early-data BIO. Between them it allocates a buffer of the maximum size, creates the SSL object and BIO chain (buffering and SSL BIOs), optionally reads early data (any read error goes to err), then loops reading request lines; a retry is retried after a one-second sleep, a read of 0 ends with goto end, and otherwise it handles GET /reneg, GET /stats, GET / and file requests, building the reply (including the directory text with escaping) and writing it, with write errors going to the write_error label that frees the file BIO and ends the request loop. After the loop it flushes io until the flush succeeds or cannot be retried.
note: s_server.c:3255-3733 checked only through grep of control flow (ret assignments at 3258 and 3417, gotos, labels at 3723 and 3727, return at 3732) and a read of 3404-3422 and 3700-3733; the request-handling code between 3420 and 3700 was not read line by line (partly read). The record was marked dropped, but www_body is a real function so it is fixed. The old note of return 0 on error and 1 on success is wrong; the second reviewer who said success sets 0 is also wrong: nothing sets 0.

name: smime_main
prose: Option-processing and input-loading part of the main function of the openssl smime command (apps/smime.c:195-745; the real name is smime_main, this slice 302-555). ret is initialised to 0 (215), not 1, and is set to 2 at 497, 3 at 612, 4 at 673, 5 at 690, 3 at 718 and 0 at 722; the function returns it at 745. So every goto end or goto opthelp taken before line 497 (option errors, a missing operation, signer or recipient, a failed random, provider, config or password step) leaves ret at 0 and returns 0 after printing the message (the opthelp label at 231 prints "Use -help" and goes to end), which is what the old prose said and what the reviewer who claimed 1 got wrong (reviewer 17 wrong). In this slice the remaining option cases store flags and strings (binary, nosigs, streaming, CRLF, random, provider, config, engine, passin, to, from and so on), the signer and key lists are built, missing -signer or recipient or file arguments go to opthelp (return 0), and app_passwd failure goes to end (0). From line 497 ret is 2: it then sets the format defaults, for encrypt it defaults the cipher to aes-256-cbc and loads each recipient certificate from the arguments (a failure goes to end with ret 2), loads the extra certificates and the decrypt recipient (failures print the OpenSSL errors and go to end with ret 2), and chooses the key file for decrypt or sign; the key itself is loaded after line 555.
note: smime.c:225-340 and 470-555 read with message lines skipped, plus ret and label greps over the whole function; 340-470 (the rest of the option cases and the validation) not read. Reviewer 17 wrong because ret is initialised to 0 (215). The old prose is right about 0 for option failures; its claim of 1 when the verify parameter object cannot be allocated is in the part of the function before this slice, which I did not read.

name: smime_main
prose: Operation part of the main function of the openssl smime command (apps/smime.c:195-745; the real name is smime_main, this slice 556-779 contains the work and the end label). ret is 2 on entry to this slice (set at 497), becomes 3 at 612 before the PKCS7 structure is built, 4 at 673 after it, 5 at 690, and 0 at 722; it is returned at 745. In this slice it loads the signing or decryption key when a key file is set (failure: end, ret 2), opens the input (failure: end, ret 2), for the read-type operations reads the PKCS7 as S/MIME, PEM or DER into a new structure (any failure goes to end with ret 2), reads detached content from -content when given, opens the output (failure: end, ret 2) and for verify builds the certificate store (failure: end, ret 2). Then ret is 3 and it builds the structure: encrypt with PKCS7_encrypt_ex, or sign (partial sign, certificates added when nocerts, then each signer loaded and added; a failure goes to end with ret 3) or resign, followed by PKCS7_final when not streaming; a NULL p7 goes to end with ret 3. With ret 4 it runs the operation: decrypt (failure: end, 4), verify (failure: end, 4; the signer certificates are then saved and a failure of that returns 5), pk7out (PEM write) or the writing of the result as S/MIME, PEM or DER (an unknown format goes to end with ret still 4; a write that returns 0 sets ret 3). When everything succeeds ret becomes 0. At end it prints the OpenSSL errors when ret is non-zero and frees the stacks, store, certificates, keys, digest and cipher, the PKCS7, engine, BIOs, password and config.
note: smime.c:556-745 read with message lines skipped. The old statements of codes 2, 3, 4 and 5 match what I read (497, 612, 673, 690); the old claim that return 3 covers failures while writing output matches 716-719 only for rv == 0.

name: process
prose: Static function of the openssl storeutl command (apps/storeutl.c:362-516) that opens a store URI and prints or writes every item; it returns an int that works as an error count (0 means no error found). ret starts at 1. If OSSL_STORE_open_ex fails it prints the errors and returns 1 immediately, without closing anything. If expected is non-zero and OSSL_STORE_expect fails, or a search criterion is given and the store does not support it or OSSL_STORE_find fails, it goes to end2 with ret 1. Otherwise ret is set to 0 and the loop calls OSSL_STORE_load repeatedly. A NULL item with an error indication clears the error queue when recursive is set (otherwise prints it), ends the loop if the store is at end-of-file, and otherwise adds 1 to ret and continues (so recursive load errors are cleared but still counted, reviewer 2 right). A NULL item without error ends the loop at end-of-file, or prints "returned NULL without eof or error", adds 1 and ends the loop. For each item it prints its index and type (and name and description for a name item) to bio_out, opens the global output BIO out on first use (failure: ret is incremented and it goes to end2 without freeing the current item, reviewer 15 right). For name items with recursive it adds the result of the nested process call at an indent of two more; params, public key, private key, certificate and CRL items are printed when text is set and written in PEM when noout is not set, and the return values of these print and write calls are not checked (reviewer 1 right); an unknown type adds 1 to ret. Each handled item is freed and counted. After the loop it prints "Total found" and at end2 it closes the store, adding 1 to ret and printing the errors if the close fails, and returns ret.
note: storeutl.c:362-516 read in full with message lines skipped. The old statement that every item is freed is wrong for the bio_open_default failure (442-446 jumps to end2 before OSSL_STORE_INFO_free at 505). Reviewers 1, 2 and 15 right on write errors not checked (465-497), counted recursive load errors (409-416) and the leaked item.

name: print_x509v3_exts
prose: Static function of the openssl x509 command (apps/x509.c:1304-1365; the real name is print_x509v3_exts, with arguments bio, x and ext_names) that prints the extensions of a certificate whose short names appear in a comma-separated list. It returns an int: ret starts at 0. If the certificate has no extensions it prints "No extensions in certificate" to bio_err and returns 1. It duplicates ext_names and parses the list in place (an allocation failure returns 0; zero parsed names prints "Invalid extension names" to bio and returns 0), allocates the name array (failure: 0) and fills it. For each extension of the certificate with a known short name that equals one of the listed names it pushes the extension onto a new stack exts2 (an allocation or push failure returns 0); an extension that matches several names is pushed once per match. It then tests sk_X509_EXTENSION_num(exts2) with !: when exts2 was created and is empty this cannot happen, but when nothing matched exts2 is still NULL and OPENSSL_sk_num(NULL) is -1, so the test is false, the "No extensions matched" message is not printed, and the call X509V3_extensions_print(bio, NULL, NULL, 0, 0) runs, which returns 1 for an empty or NULL stack; so the no-match result is 1 without that message. Otherwise ret is the result of X509V3_extensions_print for the matched extensions. At end it frees the stack exts2 (not the extensions themselves), the names array and the duplicated string.
note: x509.c:1304-1365 read in full; stack.c:452-455 (OPENSSL_sk_num returns -1 for NULL) and v3_prn.c (X509V3_extensions_print returns 1 when the stack count is at most 0) checked. The packet name is a placeholder; the function is print_x509v3_exts (1304). Reviewer 17 right that the "No extensions matched" message is not printed when no extension matched (1353-1357), the final return is 1 through the print call.

name: AES_bi_ige_encrypt
prose: Bidirectional IGE-mode AES transform (crypto/aes/aes_ige.c:180-295; the real name is AES_bi_ige_encrypt, which returns nothing; the slice 275-295 is only the second loop of its decrypt branch). It checks with OPENSSL_assert that in, out, key and ivec are non-NULL, that enc is AES_ENCRYPT or AES_DECRYPT and that length is a multiple of the AES block size (a violation aborts). For encryption it first runs a forward IGE pass over the data from in to out starting with the pair ivec and ivec+16, then a backward pass in place on out from the last block to the first with the pair ivec+32 and ivec+48. For decryption it runs a backward pass from the last block of in to out with the pair ivec+32 and ivec+48, and then a forward pass in place over out with the pair ivec and ivec+16 (the slice). All block operations use AES_encrypt or AES_decrypt with key only: the parameter key2 is not used anywhere in the function (reviewer 17 wrong that the backward pass uses it). ivec is const and is not modified; in is only read except where it overlaps out.
note: aes_ige.c:180-295 read in full, comments skipped. Packet name cbc_decrypt_forwards_loop does not exist; the function is AES_bi_ige_encrypt (180). Reviewer 17 wrong: every AES_encrypt and AES_decrypt call in 207-293 passes key.

name: ossl_c2i_ASN1_OBJECT
prose: Decodes the content octets of an ASN.1 OBJECT IDENTIFIER into an ASN1_OBJECT (crypto/asn1/a_object.c:238-331; the real name is ossl_c2i_ASN1_OBJECT with arguments a, pp and len; the slice 287-380 shows its second half and then ASN1_OBJECT_new, ASN1_OBJECT_free and ASN1_OBJECT_create). It returns NULL, raising ASN1_R_INVALID_OBJECT_ENCODING, if len is not positive or exceeds INT_MAX, pp or *pp is NULL, or the last content byte has its high bit set; it also returns NULL with the same error if any sub-identifier starts with the padding byte 0x80. If the bytes match a known object (OBJ_obj2nid is not NID_undef) it returns that static object from OBJ_nid2obj, frees *a first when a is non-NULL (ASN1_OBJECT_free frees only a dynamic object) and stores the static object in *a, and advances *pp by len. Otherwise it creates a new object with ASN1_OBJECT_new when a is NULL, *a is NULL or *a is not marked dynamic (NULL on allocation failure, without an error raised here), else reuses *a. It takes the old data pointer out of the object, and when there was none or the old length is smaller than length it frees it, sets the length to 0, allocates a new length-byte buffer (failure: err) and sets the dynamic-data flag. It copies the bytes, frees the old sn and ln when the dynamic-strings flag is set and clears it, stores the new data and length, clears sn and ln, advances *pp past the bytes and stores the object in *a when a is non-NULL, and returns it. At err it raises an ASN1 error whose reason value is the local variable i (which holds length after the loop), frees the new object unless it is *a, and returns NULL; in the reuse case a failed allocation leaves *a with data NULL and length 0 and *pp not advanced.
note: a_object.c:225-380 read in full, comments skipped. Packet name c2i_ASN1_OBJECT is the public wrapper at about 200-236 (it checks the tag and calls ossl_c2i_ASN1_OBJECT); this slice and the old prose describe the callee ossl_c2i_ASN1_OBJECT, whose real name is used. The reason code at 327 is i, which is not a named error constant (observation, no reviewer claim).

name: ASN1_item_sign_ctx
prose: Signs the DER encoding of an ASN.1 item with an already initialised EVP_MD_CTX (crypto/asn1/a_sign.c:146-288) and returns an int: the length of the signature stored in signature on the normal success path, and 0 on most failures with an error raised. It takes the digest and the key from the context; if the context has no key it raises ASN1_R_CONTEXT_NOT_INITIALISED and returns 0. If the key has no legacy method table (pkey->ameth is NULL, a provider key) it requires a signature operation context, asks the provider for the signature algorithm identifier (a failure or an empty identifier returns 0), decodes that identifier into algor1 and algor2 when those are non-NULL (a decode failure returns 0) and goes on to sign with rv equal to 3. If the method has an item_sign hook it calls it: a result of 1 sets outl to the signature length and returns it at once through the cleanup, without allocating or re-setting anything, so the hook has already filled signature and ASN1_item_sign_ctx only reports its length (reviewer 15 right, the unused-bits count is not set here); a result of 0 or below raises ERR_R_EVP_LIB and returns 0; a result of 2 continues with the generic code. Without a hook rv is 2. In the generic case (rv 2) it requires a digest (else error and 0), looks up the signature algorithm id from the digest and key type (not found: error, 0), and sets algor1 and algor2 when they are non-NULL (failure: 0). It then DER-encodes the item (a non-positive length raises an error and returns 0), asks EVP_DigestSign for the signature size, allocates the output buffer (failure returns 0), signs, stores the buffer into signature with ASN1_STRING_set0 and sets its unused-bits count to 0; the buffer is owned by signature after that. The cleanup at the err label clears and frees the input buffer and the output buffer (when it was not handed over). The return value is outl, which the function sets to the signature length only at the points described and to 0 on the other error paths.
note: a_sign.c:113-288 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 wrong (the function returns the signature length, not 1 or the rv values 1, 2, 3, which are internal); reviewer 15 right (209-211 and 221-222 return signature->length without any allocation or bits_left change). Wording on rv 2 coming back from item_sign relies on the comment at 212-218, which I skipped.

name: ASN1_object_size
prose: Returns the total encoded size of an ASN.1 element (crypto/asn1/asn1_lib.c:222-249), as an int, or -1. Arguments are constructed, length (content length) and tag. It returns -1 at once when length is negative. Otherwise it starts with a header size of 1 and, when tag is 31 or more, adds one for each base-128 digit of the tag (1 for 31 to 127, 2 up to 16383, 3 up to 2097151, 4 up to 268435455 and 5 above that); when constructed is exactly 2 (indefinite length) it adds 3 (a length octet and the two end-of-contents octets); otherwise it adds 1 for the length octet and, when length exceeds 127, one more for each byte of the length (1 up to 255, 2 up to 65535, 3 up to 16777215, 4 above). If the header size is at least INT_MAX minus length it returns -1; otherwise it returns the header size plus length. It reads no state and allocates nothing.
note: asn1_lib.c:222-249 read in full. Contract rewritten with conditional terms only, because the previous one added boolean comparisons to integers, which Frama-C rejected (round 15); the values match the loops at 228-245 (base-128 digits for the tag, base-256 digits for the length).

name: asn1_item_embed_new
prose: Creates and initialises a new ASN.1 value for the item it (crypto/asn1/tasn_new.c:57-170; static int, with pval, it, embed, libctx and propq; the slice is the whole file start). If the item has an auxiliary callback it is kept in asn1_cb. It switches on the item type. EXTERN: if the extern functions exist, it calls asn1_ex_new_ex, or else asn1_ex_new when that exists, and a failure goes to asn1err; when there are no functions or neither callback exists it does nothing at all and returns 1 without touching *pval (reviewer 15 right). PRIMITIVE: uses asn1_template_new when the item has a template, otherwise asn1_primitive_new, with failure going to asn1err. MSTRING: asn1_primitive_new, failure to asn1err. CHOICE and SEQUENCE/NDEF_SEQUENCE: first the NEW_PRE callback, whose result 0 goes to auxerr and 2 makes the function return 1 right away with *pval untouched; then it zeroes the storage in place when embed is set, otherwise allocates it with OPENSSL_zalloc, where an allocation failure returns 0 immediately with *pval NULL and no error raised (reviewer 1 right). A CHOICE sets its selector to -1; a SEQUENCE initialises the lock (failure frees a non-embedded allocation, sets *pval to NULL and goes to asn1err), initialises the encoding cache and creates every field with asn1_template_new (a failure goes to asn1err2). The NEW_POST callback failing goes to auxerr2. The error labels: asn1err2 and auxerr2 free the partly built value with ossl_asn1_item_embed_free and then raise ERR_R_ASN1_LIB (asn1err) or ASN1_R_AUX_ERROR (auxerr) and return 0; asn1err and auxerr alone raise the error and return 0 without freeing. So partial state is freed only on the SEQUENCE field failure and on NEW_POST failure, not on EXTERN, PRIMITIVE, MSTRING or NEW_PRE failure. All other item types return 1 without doing anything. Otherwise it returns 1 after the switch.
note: tasn_new.c:57-170 read in full, comments skipped; the head lines (57-60) were not read, the parameter list is from the callers' use. Reviewers 1 and 15 right: allocation failure returns 0 with no error raised (113-115, 135-137), and the EXTERN no-callback path returns 1 without touching *pval (77-86).

name: IMPLEMENT_ASN1_STRING_FUNCTIONS
prose: Macro (crypto/asn1/tasn_typ.c:16-26) that defines the item, encode functions and the allocator pair for an ASN.1 string type sname; this record is its instance for ASN1_OCTET_STRING (line 28). The generated function ASN1_OCTET_STRING_new(void) takes no arguments and returns ASN1_STRING_type_new(V_ASN1_OCTET_STRING): a newly allocated string object of that type owned by the caller, or NULL when the allocation fails. It touches no global state.
note: tasn_typ.c:16-28 read. The packet name ASN1_OCTET_STRING_new is generated by the macro IMPLEMENT_ASN1_STRING_FUNCTIONS, so the macro head is the name used here; the instance is at line 28. Callee ASN1_STRING_type_new not read.

name: IMPLEMENT_ASN1_STRING_FUNCTIONS
prose: Macro (crypto/asn1/tasn_typ.c:16-26) that defines the item, encode functions and the allocator pair for an ASN.1 string type sname; this record is the free function generated for ASN1_OCTET_STRING (line 28). ASN1_OCTET_STRING_free(ASN1_OCTET_STRING *x) returns nothing and calls ASN1_STRING_free(x) with x unchanged, so for NULL it does nothing further than what ASN1_STRING_free does with NULL (not read here), and after the call x must not be used by the caller.
note: tasn_typ.c:23-28 read. Name is the macro head because the function is macro-generated; ASN1_STRING_free body not read, so the NULL case is not asserted.

name: IMPLEMENT_ASN1_STRING_FUNCTIONS
prose: Macro (crypto/asn1/tasn_typ.c:16-26) that defines the item, encode functions and the allocator pair for an ASN.1 string type sname; this record is its instance for ASN1_INTEGER (line 29). The generated function ASN1_INTEGER_new(void) takes no arguments and returns ASN1_STRING_type_new(V_ASN1_INTEGER): a newly allocated string object of that type owned by the caller, or NULL when the allocation fails. name: buffer_ctrl
prose: Control function of the buffering BIO (crypto/bio/bf_buff.c:235-409; static long buffer_ctrl(BIO *b, int cmd, long num, void *ptr), the slice 302-468 also contains buffer_callback_ctrl, buffer_gets and buffer_puts, which are not described here). It reads the context from b->ptr and starts with ret equal to 1. By command: RESET clears the four buffer offsets and lengths, returns 0 when there is no next BIO and otherwise returns the next BIO's result; EOF returns 0 if buffered input remains and otherwise the next BIO's answer (the next BIO is not checked for NULL here); INFO returns the output length; GET_BUFF_NUM_LINES counts newlines in the buffered input; WPENDING and PENDING return the buffered output or input length, or, when that is 0, 0 for a missing next BIO and otherwise the next BIO's answer; SET_BUFF_READ_DATA enlarges the input buffer when num exceeds its size (a non-positive num or an allocation failure returns 0), then resets the offset, sets the length to num and copies num bytes from ptr, returning 1; SET_BUFF_SIZE takes the input size, the output size or both from ptr and num (ptr pointing to 0 selects input, other values select output, NULL selects both), allocates a new buffer only when the requested size is above DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE and differs from the current one (the first branch returns 0 for a non-positive num or an allocation failure, the second frees the first new buffer when it fails and returns 0), swaps in the new buffers, resets their offsets and lengths and updates only their size fields, and returns 1; DO_STATE_MACHINE returns 0 without a next BIO and otherwise forwards and copies the retry flags; FLUSH returns 0 without a next BIO, forwards at once when no output is pending, and otherwise writes out the pending output in a loop (a write result of 0 or less is returned as the result, with the retry flags copied) and then forwards the flush to the next BIO; DUP sets the duplicate's read and write buffer sizes and gives 0 if either fails, else 1; PEEK first calls buffer_read with a zero length to fill the buffer, limits num to the buffered input length, copies that many bytes to ptr without consuming them and returns that count; any other command returns 0 without a next BIO and otherwise the next BIO's answer.
note: bf_buff.c:205-409 read in full, comments skipped. The old prose matches these cases; it did not mention that SET_BUFF_SIZE leaves the size fields of non-reallocated buffers unchanged, which the code confirms (335-348). Reviewer-less record (fixed-unreviewed).

name: prefix_write
prose: Write method of the prefix BIO (crypto/bio/bf_prefix.c:81-149; static int prefix_write(BIO *b, const char *out, size_t outl, size_t *numwritten), returning 1 on success and 0 on failure). It takes the context from the BIO data pointer and returns 0 at once, leaving *numwritten untouched, when the context is NULL. When no prefix is set (NULL or empty) and the indent is 0 it records whether the last byte of out is a newline in ctx->linestart (only when outl is positive) and returns the result of BIO_write_ex on the next BIO, with *numwritten set by that call. Otherwise it sets *numwritten to 0 and loops while bytes remain: at the start of a line it writes the prefix (a failed prefix write returns 0 at once), then prints the indent as that many spaces with BIO_printf, whose result is not checked (reviewer 1 right), and clears linestart. It then takes the bytes up to and including the next newline (or all the rest), writes them with BIO_write_ex in a loop that handles partial writes, adding each successful count to *numwritten, and returns 0 when a write fails, so on failure *numwritten holds the total of bytes successfully written before the failing call, not the count of the last call (reviewer 15 right). After a chunk ending in a newline it sets linestart again. It returns 1 after consuming all outl bytes (also for outl equal to 0, with *numwritten 0).
note: bf_prefix.c:76-149 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (121 ignores the BIO_printf result); reviewer 15 right (139 accumulates successful counts only).

name: readbuffer_gets
prose: Gets one line (or up to size minus 1 bytes) from the read-buffering BIO (crypto/bio/bf_readbuff.c:218-291; static int readbuffer_gets(BIO *b, char *buf, int size), the real name of the function whose tail the slice 262-291 shows; there is no function buffer_read in this slice). It returns 0 when buf is NULL or size is 0, and, after reserving one byte for the terminator, when the context is NULL or there is no next BIO. It clears the retry flags and first copies already buffered bytes from ctx->ibuf up to size or the first newline, advancing the offset and reducing the buffered length; if it found a newline or the size is used up it writes the terminator and returns the count. Otherwise it calls readbuffer_resize(ctx, 1 + size) and returns 0 when that fails (buf is then not terminated, and bytes copied earlier remain in buf). It then reads from the next BIO one byte at a time into the buffer and buf, advancing ibuf_off, until size bytes are read or a newline was read; a read result of 0 or less copies the next BIO's retry flags, terminates buf and returns the number of bytes read so far if positive and otherwise that read result. Normal completion terminates buf and returns the number of bytes copied. For size equal to 1 it terminates buf and returns 0. It takes no ownership.
note: bf_readbuff.c:218-291 read in full, comments skipped; readbuffer_resize was not read, so what a failed resize leaves in the context is not claimed. The old prose called the function buffer_read; the real name is readbuffer_gets (218). It read one byte per call from the next BIO, which matches 275-288.

name: BIO_lookup_ex
prose: Resolves a host and service into a list of address records (crypto/bio/bio_addr.c:680-968; the real name is BIO_lookup_ex, with host, service, lookup_type, family, socktype, protocol and res; the slice 803-970 is the legacy gethostbyname branch near its end). It returns an int, 1 on success and 0 on failure, starting with ret equal to 0. It first rejects, with BIO_R_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_FAMILY and 0, any family other than AF_INET, AF_INET6 (when IPv6 is enabled), AF_UNIX (when enabled) and AF_UNSPEC. For AF_UNIX it wraps the host string as a unix address with addrinfo_wrap and returns 1 on success, or raises ERR_R_BIO_LIB and returns 0. Otherwise it calls BIO_sock_init and returns 0 if that is not 1. When AI_PASSIVE is defined (the usual case) the structure is "if (1) { getaddrinfo path } else { legacy path }", so the legacy code in the slice is never compiled in as reachable: the getaddrinfo path fills a hints structure from family, socktype and protocol (AI_ADDRCONFIG for a host with an unspecified family, AI_PASSIVE for a server lookup), calls getaddrinfo, treats 0 as success (ret 1), raises a system or BIO error for EAI_SYSTEM, EAI_MEMORY and other codes, and on another error retries once with AI_NUMERICHOST instead of AI_ADDRCONFIG. In the legacy branch (used when AI_PASSIVE is not defined) it runs the one-time lock initialisation (failure: error and 0), takes the write lock (failure: 0 with no error raised), and takes the host from a fallback address (loopback for a client lookup, any for a server lookup, an unknown lookup type asserts and raises ERR_R_INTERNAL_ERROR with ret 0) or from gethostbyname (failure raises a system error 1000 plus h_errno, or 1000 on VxWorks, or the socket error on Windows, with ret 0). It takes the port from a numeric service (1 to 65535) or, for a non-numeric service, from getservbyname with "tcp" for SOCK_STREAM, "udp" for SOCK_DGRAM or NULL otherwise; a failure of that lookup goes to the unlock with ret still 0, and a service that starts numeric but is malformed raises BIO_R_MALFORMED_HOST_OR_SERVICE, also with ret 0. It then builds a list of address records from the back of the host address list with addrinfo_wrap; on a wrap failure it frees the list, sets *res to NULL and returns 0. On success *res is the new list (to be freed with BIO_ADDRINFO_free) and ret is 1. The legacy-branch paths that acquired the lock release it at the err label (a failed lock acquisition returns before that), and the function returns ret.
note: bio_addr.c:680-968 read with preprocessor details skimmed. In the getaddrinfo branch, on failure *res may have been left by getaddrinfo (not written by this code); the legacy part is only active without AI_PASSIVE (715 and 771-772), a point the old prose did not mention. The old prose is otherwise right on the error values; the claim that the lock is released on every path that acquired it matches 963-964. The packet name bio_lookup_ex does not exist in that case, the function is BIO_lookup_ex.
